part3: Part Three: Walking the Mediterranean World
ch12.title: From Joppa to Alexandria
ch12.b002: On a Sunday morning, April 26, A.D. 22, Jesus and the two travelers from India, Gonod and his son Ganid, left Jerusalem. The tour of the Roman world would consume most of his twenty-eighth year and the whole of his twenty-ninth, and it would end only on December 10 of the following year, in the city of Charax on the Persian Gulf, where Jesus said good-bye to father and son. The route was long: Joppa and Caesarea, then by sea to Alexandria, to Lasea in Crete, to Carthage by way of Cyrene, to Naples by way of Malta, Syracuse, and Messina, and up the Appian Way to Rome. Afterward would come Tarentum, Nicopolis, Corinth, Athens, Troas, Ephesus, Rhodes, Cyprus, Antioch, Sidon, Damascus, and at last the long caravan road to Mesopotamia, Babylon, Ur, Susa, and Charax.
ch12.b003: Jesus had picked up the rudiments of their language during his four months in Damascus, where he had worked much of the time translating Greek into one of the languages of India. Now, about half of each day, he taught Ganid and acted as interpreter in Gonod’s business conferences and social contacts. The rest of the day was his own, and he gave it to those close personal contacts with his fellow men which so characterized the years just before his public ministry. From firsthand observation he came to know the higher civilization of the Occident and the Levant; from Gonod, who had made three long journeys to China, and from his brilliant son, he learned much of the culture of India and China. Ganid learned much from Jesus, and a great affection grew between them. Many times the father urged Jesus to return with them to India, but he always declined, pleading the necessity of returning to his family in Palestine.
ch12.b005: At Joppa they visited one Simon a tanner, with whom Gonod’s agents in Mesopotamia had done much business, and there Jesus met Gadiah, a Philistine interpreter who worked for Simon. The two became warm friends. The young Philistine was a truth seeker, and Jesus was a truth giver; when a great truth seeker and a great truth giver meet, the result is a great and liberating enlightenment. One day after the evening meal they strolled down by the sea, the waves washing softly against the old stones of the harbor, and Gadiah, not knowing how well this “scribe of Damascus” knew the Hebrew traditions, pointed out the ship landing from which Jonah was said to have set out for Tarshish. Then he asked: “⟦Q 130:1.2⟧But do you suppose the big fish really did swallow Jonah?⟦/Q⟧”
ch12.b006: Jesus perceived that this tradition had deeply influenced the young man’s life and had impressed upon him the folly of running away from duty, so he said nothing that would suddenly destroy the foundations of Gadiah’s motivation for practical living. He answered:

ch12.b007.en: “My friend, we are all Jonahs with lives to live in accordance with the will of God, and at all times when we seek to escape the present duty of living by running away to far-off enticements, we thereby put ourselves in the immediate control of those influences which are not directed by the powers of truth and the forces of righteousness. The flight from duty is the sacrifice of truth. … No matter into what great depths they may have fallen, when they seek the light with a whole heart, the spirit of the Lord God of heaven will deliver them from their captivity; the evil circumstances of life will spew them out upon the dry land of fresh opportunities for renewed service and wiser living.”

ch12.b008: Gadiah was mightily moved. They talked long into the night by the seaside, and before they went to their lodgings, they prayed together and for each other. This was the same Gadiah who later heard Peter preach, became a profound believer in Jesus of Nazareth, and held a memorable argument with Peter one evening at the home of Dorcas; and he had much to do with the final decision of Simon the leather merchant to embrace Christianity.
ch12.b009: Their last visit together turned on good and evil. Gadiah was troubled by the presence of evil in the world alongside the good. “⟦Q 130:1.5⟧How can God, if he is infinitely good, permit us to suffer the sorrows of evil; after all, who creates evil?⟦/Q⟧” Many still believed that God creates both good and evil, but Jesus never taught such error. He said: “⟦Q 130:1.5⟧My brother, God is love; therefore he must be good, and his goodness is so great and real that it cannot contain the small and unreal things of evil. … Evil is the inevitable darkness which follows upon the heels of the unwise rejection of light.⟦/Q⟧” The Father, by giving his children the power to choose between truth and error, had created the potential negative of the way of light; but such evils are really nonexistent until an intelligent creature wills their existence by mischoosing. “⟦Q 130:1.6⟧This is why our Father in heaven permits the good and the evil to go along together until the end of life, just as nature allows the wheat and the tares to grow side by side until the harvest.⟦/Q⟧” After further talk had made the meaning clear, Gadiah was fully satisfied.
ch12.b011: At Caesarea they were delayed beyond their plans, for one of the huge steering paddles of their ship was found to be in danger of cleaving, and the captain stayed in port while a new one was made. Skilled woodworkers were scarce, so Jesus volunteered to help. In the evenings the three strolled on the beautiful wall that served as a promenade around the port, and Ganid delighted in Jesus’ explanation of how the tides were used to flush the city’s streets and sewers. The youth was much impressed by the temple of Augustus with its colossal statue of the emperor. On the second afternoon the three attended a performance in the amphitheater that seated twenty thousand, and that night they saw a Greek play, the first such exhibitions Ganid had ever witnessed. They also paid a formal visit to the governor’s palace, for Caesarea was the residence of the Roman procurator. At their inn Jesus had several long visits with a Taoist merchant from Mongolia, who never forgot his words about “⟦Q 130:2.2⟧the living of the heavenly life while on earth by means of daily submission to the will of the heavenly Father,⟦/Q⟧” and who carried these truths home to his own people.
ch12.b012: One of the young men who worked beside Jesus on the paddle, a Greek named Anaxand, grew interested in the words he dropped from hour to hour in the shipyard. When Jesus intimated that the Father in heaven cared for the welfare of his children, Anaxand said: “⟦Q 130:2.4⟧If the Gods are interested in me, then why do they not remove the cruel and unjust foreman of this workshop?⟦/Q⟧” He was startled by the reply: “⟦Q 130:2.4⟧Since you know the ways of kindness and value justice, perhaps the Gods have brought this erring man near that you may lead him into this better way. Maybe you are the salt which is to make this brother more agreeable to all other men; that is, if you have not lost your savor. … It is a marvelous and transforming experience to become the living channel of spiritual light to the mortal who sits in spiritual darkness.⟦/Q⟧” Anaxand told his foreman what Jesus had said, and that night both of them sought Jesus’ advice about their souls. Later both believed Philip’s preaching in Caesarea, and Anaxand became steward to the centurion Cornelius. He ministered light to those in darkness until he perished, by accident, in the great slaughter of twenty thousand Jews while caring for the suffering and dying.
ch12.b013: By now Ganid was beginning to see how his tutor spent his leisure, and he asked, “⟦Q 130:2.6⟧Why do you occupy yourself so continuously with these visits with strangers?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus answered: “⟦Q 130:2.6⟧Ganid, no man is a stranger to one who knows God. In the experience of finding the Father in heaven you discover that all men are your brothers, and does it seem strange that one should enjoy the exhilaration of meeting a newly discovered brother? To become acquainted with one’s brothers and sisters, to know their problems and to learn to love them, is the supreme experience of living.⟦/Q⟧”
ch12.b014: That conversation lasted well into the night. Ganid asked the difference between the will of God and the human act of choosing which is also called will, and Jesus said in substance that the will of God is the way of God, partnership with the choice of God, while the will of man is the sum of what a mortal chooses to be and do. That afternoon they had played with a very intelligent shepherd dog, and Ganid wanted to know whether the dog had a soul and a will. Jesus explained that the dog has a mind which can know its master but cannot know God, who is spirit; its will is not reflective, not a choosing of moral meanings and spiritual values. After that day Ganid never again believed in the transmigration of the souls of men into the bodies of animals. It was then, too, that the revelators first heard the truth which, stated in modern terms, would signify: “⟦Q 130:2.10⟧Will is that manifestation of the human mind which enables the subjective consciousness to express itself objectively and to experience the phenomenon of aspiring to be Godlike.⟦/Q⟧”
ch12.b016: When the paddle was ready, they sailed at noon one day for Alexandria. Ganid was delighted with the voyage and kept Jesus busy answering questions. As they approached the harbor, the young man was thrilled by the great lighthouse of Pharos, standing on the island that Alexander had joined to the mainland by a mole, creating two magnificent harbors and making the city the maritime crossroads of Africa, Asia, and Europe. This lighthouse was one of the seven wonders of the world. They rose early to see it in the morning light, its tower rising white above the blue water, and amid Ganid’s exclamations Jesus said: “⟦Q 130:3.2⟧And you, my son, will be like this lighthouse when you return to India, even after your father is laid to rest; you will become like the light of life to those who sit about you in darkness, showing all who so desire the way to reach the harbor of salvation in safety.⟦/Q⟧” And Ganid squeezed his hand and said, “I will.”
ch12.b018: They settled near the eastern end of the great avenue, a hundred feet wide and five miles long, that ran through this city of a million people. After a survey of the university, the library, the royal mausoleum of Alexander, the palace, the temple of Neptune, the theater, and the gymnasium, Gonod turned to business, while Jesus and Ganid went to the library, the greatest in the world. Nearly a million manuscripts were gathered there from Greece, Rome, Palestine, Parthia, India, China, and even Japan, and Ganid found the largest collection of Indian literature anywhere. They spent time there every day. Jesus told the lad how the Hebrew scriptures had been translated into Greek in that very city. They discussed the religions of the world again and again, Jesus pointing out the truth in each, but always adding: “⟦Q 130:3.4⟧But Yahweh is the God developed from the revelations of Melchizedek and the covenant of Abraham.⟦/Q⟧” The religion of the Jews, he said, “⟦Q 130:3.4⟧eventually portrayed a clearer recognition of the Lord God of Israel as the Universal Father in heaven than any other world religion.⟦/Q⟧”
ch12.b019: Under Jesus’ direction Ganid made a collection of the teachings of all the religions that recognized a Universal Deity. They concluded that the Romans had no real God, their religion being hardly more than emperor worship; that the Greeks had a philosophy but hardly a religion with a personal God; and they set aside the mystery cults because of their confused multiplicity. Ganid would arrange these selections and add his own conclusions only near the end of their stay in Rome, and he was surprised to find that the best authors of the world’s sacred literature all more or less clearly recognized an eternal God and largely agreed about his character.
ch12.b020: They spent much time also in the museum, not a collection of rare objects but a university of art, science, and literature, the intellectual center of the Occident. Jesus interpreted the daily lectures for Ganid, and one day in the second week the young man exclaimed: “⟦Q 130:3.7⟧Teacher Joshua, you know more than these professors; you should stand up and tell them the great things you have told me; they are befogged by much thinking. I shall speak to my father and have him arrange it.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus smiled and said: “⟦Q 130:3.7⟧You are an admiring pupil, but these teachers are not minded that you and I should instruct them. The pride of unspiritualized learning is a treacherous thing in human experience. The true teacher maintains his intellectual integrity by ever remaining a learner.⟦/Q⟧” Among Gonod’s business associates was a Jewish banker, Alexander, whose brother Philo was the famous philosopher then trying to harmonize Greek philosophy and Hebrew theology. Jesus and Ganid hoped to hear him lecture, but throughout their stay Philo lay sick abed.
ch12.b022: On their last night in Alexandria Ganid and Jesus had a long visit with one of the university professors who lectured on Plato. Jesus interpreted for him but injected no teaching of his own. Gonod was away on business, and after the professor had gone, teacher and pupil talked far into the night. Jesus gave qualified approval to the idea that material things are shadowy reflections of invisible spiritual realities, but he sought to lay a more trustworthy foundation for the lad’s thinking, and he spoke at length on the nature of reality. The source of universe reality, he said in substance, is the Infinite. “⟦Q 130:4.4⟧A one-eyed person can never hope to visualize depth of perspective,⟦/Q⟧” and neither can single-eyed materialists nor single-eyed mystics comprehend the true depths of reality. Personality is that endowment which can coexist with unlimited change and yet retain its identity forever. “⟦Q 130:4.7⟧The meaning of life is its adaptability; the value of life is its progressability—even to the heights of God-consciousness.⟦/Q⟧”
ch12.b023: He set knowledge and truth side by side: “⟦Q 130:4.10⟧Knowledge is demonstrable; truth is experienced. Knowledge is a possession of the mind; truth an experience of the soul, the progressing self.⟦/Q⟧” The eye of the material mind perceives a world of facts; the eye of the spiritualized intellect discerns a world of true values; and these two views, harmonized, reveal the world of reality, in which wisdom interprets the universe in terms of personal experience. Error, he explained, is the shadow of relative incompleteness that must fall across man’s ascending path to Paradise perfection. Though Jesus spoke in language suited to the lad, by the end Ganid was heavy of eye and soon fell asleep.
ch12.b024: They rose early to board the boat for Lasea in Crete, but before they embarked, Ganid had still more questions about evil. Evil, Jesus told him, is a relativity concept, arising from the imperfections seen in the shadow cast by a finite universe as it obscures the living light of the Infinite. “⟦Q 130:4.15⟧All static, dead, concepts are potentially evil. The finite shadow of relative and living truth is continually moving.⟦/Q⟧” Static concepts retard science, politics, society, and religion; they may hold some knowledge, but they lack wisdom and truth. Yet the lad was not to let the idea of relativity mislead him into overlooking the co-ordination of the universe under the guidance of the cosmic mind and the control of the Supreme. Then they went down to the harbor, the great light of Pharos behind them, and set out across the sea.
ch13.title: The Young Man Who Was Afraid
ch13.b002: The travelers had only one purpose in going to Crete: to play, to walk about the island, and to climb its mountains. The Cretans of that day did not enjoy an enviable reputation among the surrounding peoples, yet Jesus and Ganid won many souls there to higher levels of thinking and living, and so laid the foundation for the quick reception of the gospel when the first preachers from Jerusalem arrived. Jesus loved these Cretans, notwithstanding the harsh words Paul would later speak of them when he sent Titus to reorganize their churches. Day after day the three climbed among the rocky slopes, with the sea spread blue below them.
ch13.b003: On a mountainside in Crete Jesus had his first long talk with Gonod about religion, and the father was much impressed. “⟦Q 130:5.2⟧No wonder the boy believes everything you tell him,⟦/Q⟧” he said, “⟦Q 130:5.2⟧but I never knew they had such a religion even in Jerusalem, much less in Damascus.⟦/Q⟧” It was during this sojourn on the island that Gonod first proposed that Jesus go back to India with them, and Ganid was delighted at the thought that he might consent.
ch13.b004: One day Ganid asked Jesus why he had not devoted himself to the work of a public teacher. He answered: “⟦Q 130:5.3⟧My son, everything must await the coming of its time. You are born into the world, but no amount of anxiety and no manifestation of impatience will help you to grow up. You must, in all such matters, wait upon time. Time alone will ripen the green fruit upon the tree. Season follows season and sundown follows sunrise only with the passing of time. I am now on the way to Rome with you and your father, and that is sufficient for today. My tomorrow is wholly in the hands of my Father in heaven.⟦/Q⟧” And then he told Ganid the story of Moses and his forty years of watchful waiting and continued preparation.
ch13.b005: On the Road at Fair Havens
ch13.b006: On a visit to Fair Havens something happened that Ganid never forgot; the memory of it always made him wish he might do something to change the caste system of his native India. On the public highway a drunken degenerate was attacking a slave girl. When Jesus saw her plight, he rushed forward and drew the maiden away from the madman. While the frightened child clung to him, he held the infuriated man at a safe distance with his powerful extended right arm until the poor fellow had exhausted himself beating the air with angry blows. Ganid felt a strong impulse to help, but his father forbade him. Though they could not speak the girl’s language, she understood their act of mercy and gave token of her heartfelt gratitude as all three escorted her home.
ch13.b007: This was probably as near a personal encounter with his fellows as Jesus ever had in his whole life in the flesh. But that evening he had a difficult task trying to explain to Ganid why he had not struck the drunken man. Ganid thought the man should have been struck at least as many times as he had struck the girl.
ch13.b008: The Young Man on the Mountain
ch13.b009: While they were up in the mountains, Jesus came upon a young man who was fearful and downcast. Failing to find comfort and courage among his fellows, this youth had sought the solitude of the hills. He had grown up with a feeling of helplessness and inferiority, and these tendencies had been deepened by many hard circumstances, above all the loss of his father when he was twelve. As they met, Jesus said: “⟦Q 130:6.1⟧Greetings, my friend! why so downcast on such a beautiful day? If something has happened to distress you, perhaps I can in some manner assist you. At any rate it affords me real pleasure to proffer my services.⟦/Q⟧”
ch13.b010: The young man did not want to talk. So Jesus made a second approach to his soul. He said he understood that the youth had come up into the hills to get away from people, but would he perhaps know the trails, and the best route to Phenix? Now the youth knew these mountains very well, and he became so interested in showing the way that he marked out all the trails on the ground and explained every detail. Jesus said good-bye and made as if to go; then he suddenly turned back and said: “⟦Q 130:6.2⟧I well know you wish to be left alone with your disconsolation; but it would be neither kind nor fair for me to receive such generous help from you as to how best to find my way to Phenix and then unthinkingly to go away from you without making the least effort to answer your appealing request for help and guidance regarding the best route to the goal of destiny which you seek in your heart while you tarry here on the mountainside. As you so well know the trails to Phenix, having traversed them many times, so do I well know the way to the city of your disappointed hopes and thwarted ambitions. And since you have asked me for help, I will not disappoint you.⟦/Q⟧”
ch13.b011: The youth was almost overcome, but he managed to stammer, “⟦Q 130:6.2⟧But—I did not ask you for anything—⟦/Q⟧” And Jesus, laying a gentle hand on his shoulder, said: “⟦Q 130:6.2⟧No, son, not with words but with longing looks did you appeal to my heart. My boy, to one who loves his fellows there is an eloquent appeal for help in your countenance of discouragement and despair. Sit down with me while I tell you of the service trails and happiness highways which lead from the sorrows of self to the joys of loving activities in the brotherhood of men and in the service of the God of heaven.⟦/Q⟧”
ch13.b012: By now the young man longed to talk with him, and he knelt at Jesus’ feet, imploring him to show him the way of escape from his world of sorrow and defeat. Jesus said: “⟦Q 130:6.3⟧My friend, arise! Stand up like a man! You may be surrounded with small enemies and be retarded by many obstacles, but the big things and the real things of this world and the universe are on your side. The sun rises every morning to salute you just as it does the most powerful and prosperous man on earth.⟦/Q⟧” He pointed out that the youth had a strong body and a clear and capable mind, but that both were useless while he sat on the mountainside grieving over his misfortunes. “⟦Q 130:6.3⟧You are trying to run away from your unhappy self, but it cannot be done.⟦/Q⟧” His mind should be his courageous ally, not his master in fear, and most valuable of all was the spirit living within him, which would set him free from the fetters of fear by the power of living faith, when he knew in his heart that he was a child of God.

ch13.b013.en: “This day, my son, you are to be reborn, re-established as a man of faith, courage, and devoted service to man, for God’s sake. … Trouble will invigorate you; disappointment will spur you on; difficulties will challenge you; and obstacles will stimulate you. Arise, young man! Say farewell to the life of cringing fear and fleeing cowardice. Hasten back to duty and live your life in the flesh as a son of God, a mortal dedicated to the ennobling service of man on earth and destined to the superb and eternal service of God in eternity.”

ch13.b014: This youth was Fortune. In later years he became the leader of the Christians in Crete and the close associate of Titus in his labors for the Cretan believers.
ch13.b016: Truly rested and refreshed, the travelers sailed about noon one day for Carthage in northern Africa, stopping for two days at Cyrene. There Jesus and Ganid gave first aid to a lad named Rufus who had been injured when a loaded oxcart broke down. They carried him home to his mother. His father, Simon, little dreamed that the man whose cross he would one day bear, by orders of a Roman soldier, was the stranger who had once befriended his son.
ch13.b017: On the voyage to Carthage Jesus talked mostly of social, political, and commercial matters; hardly a word was said about religion. For the first time Gonod and Ganid discovered that he was a good storyteller, and they kept him busy with tales of his early life, learning that he had grown up in Galilee and not in Jerusalem or Damascus. Ganid had noticed that most of the people they met were drawn to Jesus, and he asked what one could do to make friends. His teacher said: “⟦Q 130:7.2⟧Become interested in your fellows; learn how to love them and watch for the opportunity to do something for them which you are sure they want done,⟦/Q⟧” and then he quoted the old Jewish proverb: “⟦Q 130:7.2⟧A man who would have friends must show himself friendly.⟦/Q⟧”
ch13.b018: At Carthage Jesus had a long and memorable talk with a Mithraic priest, a Persian educated at Alexandria who truly wished to learn, about immortality, time, and eternity. Time, Jesus said in substance, is the stream of flowing temporal events perceived by creature consciousness. On the inhabited worlds, human personality, indwelt by the Father’s spirit, is the only physically related reality that can transcend the material sequence of temporal events. To man’s limited view time appears as a succession of events, but as he ascends and progresses inward, what once seemed a succession will be seen as a whole and perfectly related cycle. “⟦Q 130:7.6⟧Space is measured by time, not time by space,⟦/Q⟧” and space is not empty; the only thing man knows that can even partially transcend it is mind. As personality passes upward and inward toward Deity-likeness, its concepts of time and space will increasingly approach the timeless and spaceless concepts of the Absolutes.
ch13.b020: The first stop on the way to Italy was Malta. There Jesus had a long talk with a downhearted young man named Claudus who had thought of taking his life. When he had finished talking with the scribe of Damascus, he said: “⟦Q 130:8.1⟧I will face life like a man; I am through playing the coward. I will go back to my people and begin all over again.⟦/Q⟧” He became an enthusiastic preacher of the Cynics, later joined Peter in proclaiming Christianity in Rome and Naples, and after Peter’s death carried the gospel to Spain. But he never knew that the man who inspired him in Malta was the Jesus he afterward proclaimed the world’s Deliverer.
ch13.b021: At Syracuse they spent a full week. The notable event there was the restoration of Ezra, a backslidden Jew who kept the tavern where they lodged. Charmed by Jesus’ approach, he asked for help to return to the faith of Israel. “⟦Q 130:8.2⟧I want to be a true son of Abraham,⟦/Q⟧” he said, “but I cannot find God.” Jesus answered: “⟦Q 130:8.2⟧If you truly want to find God, that desire is in itself evidence that you have already found him. Your trouble is not that you cannot find God, for the Father has already found you; your trouble is simply that you do not know God.⟦/Q⟧” And he reminded him of the words of Jeremiah: “⟦Q 130:8.2⟧You shall seek me and find me when you shall search for me with all your heart.⟦/Q⟧” Ezra found God, to the satisfaction of his soul, and later, with a well-to-do Greek proselyte, he built the first Christian church in Syracuse.
ch13.b022: At Messina they stopped only a day, but it was long enough to change the life of a small boy, a fruit vendor, from whom Jesus bought fruit and whom in turn he fed with the bread of life. Placing his hand on the boy’s shoulder, he said: “⟦Q 130:8.3⟧Farewell, my lad, be of good courage as you grow up to manhood and after you have fed the body learn how also to feed the soul. And my Father in heaven will be with you and go before you.⟦/Q⟧” The lad never forgot those words and the kindly look that went with them. He became a devotee of Mithraism and later turned to the Christian faith.
ch13.b023: From Naples to the Appian Way
ch13.b024: At last they reached Naples and felt that Rome was near. Gonod had much business there, and in their free hours Jesus and Ganid explored the city. Ganid was becoming adept at spotting those who seemed to be in need, and they found much poverty and gave many alms. Once Jesus gave a coin to a street beggar but would not pause to speak comfortingly to him, and Ganid never understood why. “⟦Q 130:8.4⟧Why waste words upon one who cannot perceive the meaning of what you say?⟦/Q⟧” Jesus said. “⟦Q 130:8.4⟧The spirit of the Father cannot teach and save one who has no capacity for sonship.⟦/Q⟧” He meant that the man was not of normal mind and lacked the ability to respond to spirit leading. There was no outstanding experience in Naples; Jesus and the young man simply canvassed the city and spread good cheer with many smiles upon hundreds of men, women, and children.
ch13.b025: From Naples they went to Capua and stayed three days. Then, by the Appian Way, they journeyed on beside their pack animals, the long paved road running straight between its tombs and milestones toward the north. All three were eager to see the mistress of the empire, the greatest city in all the world.
ch14.title: The People He Met in Rome
ch14.b002: Gonod carried greetings from the princes of India to Tiberius, the Roman ruler, and so on the third day after their arrival in Rome the two Indians and Jesus appeared before the emperor. The morose emperor was unusually cheerful that day and chatted long with the trio. When they had left his presence, he, referring to Jesus, remarked to the aide standing at his right, “⟦Q 132:0.1⟧If I had that fellow’s kingly bearing and gracious manner, I would be a real emperor, eh?⟦/Q⟧”
ch14.b003: In Rome Ganid kept regular hours for study and for visiting the sights of the city. His father had much business to transact, and wishing his son to become a worthy successor in managing his vast commercial interests, he began to introduce the boy to the business world. There were many citizens of India in Rome, and often one of Gonod’s own employees served as interpreter, so that Jesus had whole days to himself. He came to know this city of two million people thoroughly. He was often in the forum, the center of its political, legal, and business life. He frequently went up to the Capitolium, and as he looked on the magnificent temple of Jupiter, Juno, and Minerva, he pondered the bondage of ignorance in which these Romans were held. He spent much time too on the Palatine hill, with its imperial residence, its temple of Apollo, and its Greek and Latin libraries. The empire then embraced all southern Europe, Asia Minor, Syria, Egypt, and northwest Africa, and people of every nation of the Eastern Hemisphere could be met in its capital. His desire to study and mingle with this cosmopolitan gathering of mortals was the chief reason Jesus had consented to make the journey.
ch14.b005: Jesus learned much about men in Rome, but the most valuable experience of his six months there was his contact with the religious leaders of the capital. Before the end of the first week he had sought out the worth-while leaders of the Cynics, the Stoics, and the mystery cults, especially the Mithraic group. Whether or not he then foresaw that the Jews would reject his mission, he certainly foresaw that his messengers would soon come to Rome to proclaim the kingdom of heaven, and he set about, in the most amazing manner, to prepare the way for them. He chose five of the leading Stoics, eleven of the Cynics, and sixteen of the mystery-cult leaders, and for almost six months he spent much of his spare time in intimate association with them.
ch14.b006: His method was this. Never once did he attack their errors or even mention the flaws in their teachings. In each case he would select the truth in what they taught and then so embellish and illuminate it in their minds that in a short time this enhanced truth crowded out the associated error. So these Jesus-taught men and women were prepared to recognize similar truths when the early Christian missionaries came. Of the thirty-two, only two were unfruitful; the thirty became pivotal individuals in the establishment of Christianity in Rome, and some of them helped turn the chief Mithraic temple into the first Christian church of the city. Looking back across nineteen centuries, the revelators name three factors of paramount value in preparing the rapid spread of Christianity through Europe: the choosing and holding of Simon Peter as an apostle; the talk in Jerusalem with Stephen, whose death led to the winning of Saul of Tarsus; and the preparation of these thirty Romans.
ch14.b007: His work with them was entirely personal. The scribe of Damascus never met more than three of them at once, seldom more than two, and most often he taught them singly. Neither they nor Stephen ever realized that they had once talked with the man whose name became the subject of their religious teaching. In later years Peter, Paul, and the other Christian teachers in Rome often heard of this scribe of Damascus who had so obviously prepared the way before them. Shortly before his death Paul concluded, from the likeness of personal descriptions, that the “tentmaker of Antioch” was also the “scribe of Damascus.” Once, while preaching in Rome, Peter heard a description of the Damascus scribe and surmised that it might have been Jesus, but quickly dismissed the idea, knowing full well, as he thought, that the Master had never been in Rome.
ch14.b009: Early in his stay Jesus had an all-night talk with Angamon, the leader of the Stoics, who later became a great friend of Paul and a strong supporter of the church at Rome. In substance Jesus taught him that the standard of true values must be sought in the spiritual world and on divine levels of eternal reality. Unless the moral insight and spiritual attainment of mankind keep pace, the unlimited advance of a purely materialistic culture may become a menace to civilization. Scientists and religionists, he said, must recognize that in every age they are on trial before the bar of human need, and must eschew all warfare between themselves while they devote themselves to the service of human progress.
ch14.b010: Mardus, the acknowledged leader of the Cynics of Rome, became a great friend of the scribe of Damascus. Day after day he conversed with Jesus, and night upon night he listened to his teaching. To this sincere Cynic’s question about good and evil, Jesus answered in substance: “⟦Q 132:2.2⟧My brother, good and evil are merely words symbolizing relative levels of human comprehension of the observable universe.⟦/Q⟧” The soul that survives must make a living and personal choice between them, guided by the divine spirit the Father has sent to dwell in man’s heart. The spiritually blind man who merely follows scientific dictation, social usage, and religious dogma is in danger of becoming “⟦Q 132:2.4⟧an intellectual parrot, a social automaton, and a slave to religious authority.⟦/Q⟧” Until Paradise is attained, goodness will be more a quest than a possession. And he added: “⟦Q 132:2.10⟧The possibility of evil is necessary to moral choosing, but not the actuality thereof. A shadow is only relatively real.⟦/Q⟧”
ch14.b011: Nabon, a Greek Jew, was the foremost leader of the Mithraic cult, the chief mystery religion of Rome. He had thought to make a convert of Jesus and had even suggested that he return to Palestine as a Mithraic teacher, little realizing that Jesus was preparing him to become one of the early converts to the gospel of the kingdom. One evening they talked of truth and faith, and Jesus said in substance: “⟦Q 132:3.2⟧Truth cannot be defined with words, only by living. Truth is always more than knowledge.⟦/Q⟧” Knowledge deals with facts, wisdom with relationships, truth with reality values. There is never conflict between true knowledge and truth, only between knowledge and beliefs distorted by fear and prejudice. But truth can never become man’s possession without faith, for his thoughts, wisdom, and ideals will never rise higher than his faith, his sublime hope. Human life survives because it has a universe function, the task of finding God; and when the faith-activated soul achieves that goal, it can never end, for it has become like God, eternal. These truths went on burning in Nabon’s heart, and he was of great help to the later preachers of Jesus’ gospel.
ch14.b013: Jesus did not give all his leisure to preparing future disciples. He came into affectionate and uplifting contact with upward of five hundred people of every race and class in this largest and most cosmopolitan city of the world. In each contact he had a double purpose: to learn how they reacted to life in the flesh, and to say or do something to make that life richer. The burden of his message was always the same: the love of the heavenly Father and the truth of his mercy, with the good news that man is a faith-son of this God of love. He usually began by asking people questions and ended with their asking him. To those he taught the most, he said the least. Those who gained most were the overburdened, anxious, and dejected, who found in him a sympathetic and understanding listener; he offered them practical help for their real difficulties and always told them of the love of God. He regarded these six months as one of the richest periods of his earth life.
ch14.b014: He talked with a Roman senator on politics and statesmanship, and the senator spent the rest of his life vainly urging his colleagues to change from the idea of the government feeding the people to that of the people supporting the government. He spent one evening with a wealthy slaveholder named Claudius, speaking of man as a son of God, and the next day Claudius freed one hundred and seventeen slaves. He told a Greek physician that his patients had minds and souls as well as bodies. The only place in Rome he did not visit was the public baths, because of the sex promiscuity that prevailed there. To a Roman soldier, as they walked along the Tiber, he said: “⟦Q 132:4.6⟧Be brave of heart as well as of hand. Dare to do justice and be big enough to show mercy. Compel your lower nature to obey your higher nature as you obey your superiors. Revere goodness and exalt truth. Choose the beautiful in place of the ugly. Love your fellows and reach out for God with a whole heart, for God is your Father in heaven.⟦/Q⟧”
ch14.b015: To a speaker at the forum he said: “⟦Q 132:4.7⟧Your eloquence is pleasing, your logic is admirable, your voice is pleasant, but your teaching is hardly true. If you could only enjoy the inspiring satisfaction of knowing God as your spiritual Father, then you might employ your powers of speech to liberate your fellows from the bondage of darkness and from the slavery of ignorance.⟦/Q⟧” This was the Marcus who later heard Peter preach in Rome and became his successor, and who, when Peter was crucified, boldly went on preaching the gospel. Once Jesus met a poor man who had been falsely accused, and went with him before the magistrate. Granted special permission to speak for him, he said in the course of a superb address: “⟦Q 132:4.8⟧Justice makes a nation great, and the greater a nation the more solicitous will it be to see that injustice shall not befall even its most humble citizen. … Civil government is founded on justice, even as true religion is founded on mercy.⟦/Q⟧” The judge reopened the case and discharged the prisoner. Of all Jesus’ activities in those days, this came nearest to a public appearance.
ch14.b017: A wealthy Roman citizen, a Stoic introduced by Angamon, became greatly interested in Jesus’ teaching, and after many intimate conferences he asked what Jesus would do with wealth if he had it. Jesus answered: “⟦Q 132:5.1⟧I would administer material wealth as a wise and effective trustee of the resources of one generation for the benefit and ennoblement of the next and succeeding generations.⟦/Q⟧” Not fully satisfied, the man asked again what someone in his own position should do: keep his wealth or give it away? Perceiving that he truly wanted to know his duty to God and men, Jesus offered him counsel, stressing that it was meant for him alone and not for judging other rich men. Let him first ask honestly where his wealth had come from. Jesus named ten sources: inherited, discovered, trade, unfair, interest, genius, accidental, stolen, trust, and earned wealth.
ch14.b018: Then, through several hours, he explained how each portion should be administered. Inherited wealth should be handed on honestly, but he was not obliged to perpetuate any injustice in its origin. The honest trader might take the profit he would gladly allow a fellow trader. “⟦Q 132:5.18⟧Riches are a moral curse and a spiritual stigma when they are derived from the sweat of oppressed mortal man,⟦/Q⟧” and such wealth should be restored. Fair interest might be collected, but never usury from a brother in distress. Whatever had been gained by fraud he must make haste to restore. What represented his own honest labor was truly his own. And in doubtful cases, Jesus said: “⟦Q 132:5.13⟧When in honest doubt about the equity and justice of material situations, let your decisions favor those who are in need, favor those who suffer the misfortune of undeserved hardships.⟦/Q⟧” When he had finished, the wealthy Roman rose from his couch and said: “⟦Q 132:5.25⟧My good friend, I perceive you are a man of great wisdom and goodness, and tomorrow I will begin the administration of all my wealth in accordance with your counsel.⟦/Q⟧”
ch14.b020: In Rome, too, occurred that touching incident in which the Creator of a universe spent several hours restoring a lost child to his anxious mother. Jesus and Ganid were on their way to the libraries when they found the little boy crying in distress, and they gave themselves to getting him home. Ganid never forgot what Jesus said: “⟦Q 132:6.1⟧You know, Ganid, most human beings are like the lost child. They spend much of their time crying in fear and suffering in sorrow when, in very truth, they are but a short distance from safety and security, even as this child was only a little way from home. … Did we not supremely enjoy this ministry of restoring the child to his mother? So do those who lead men to God experience the supreme satisfaction of human service.⟦/Q⟧” From that day, for the rest of his life, Ganid was always on the lookout for lost children whom he might restore to their homes.
ch14.b021: There was also a widow with five children whose husband had been killed by accident. Jesus told Ganid of his own father’s death, and they went again and again to comfort the family, Ganid asking his father for money for food and clothing, until they had found a position for the eldest boy. That night, hearing all this, Gonod said good-naturedly: “⟦Q 132:6.3⟧I propose to make a scholar or a businessman of my son, and now you start out to make a philosopher or philanthropist of him.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus smiled and said: “⟦Q 132:6.3⟧Perhaps we will make him all four; then can he enjoy a fourfold satisfaction in life as his ear for the recognition of human melody will be able to recognize four tones instead of one.⟦/Q⟧” Gonod said, “⟦Q 132:6.3⟧I perceive that you really are a philosopher. You must write a book for future generations.⟦/Q⟧” And Jesus replied: “⟦Q 132:6.3⟧Not a book—my mission is to live a life in this generation and for all generations. I—⟦/Q⟧” but he stopped, saying to Ganid, “⟦Q 132:6.3⟧My son, it is time to retire.⟦/Q⟧”
ch14.b023: During these months Ganid finished a work he had begun at Alexandria. With much of his time, no small sum of his father’s money, and more than threescore learned translators, he had collected the teachings of the world’s religions about God and his relation to mortal man, under ten heads: Cynicism, Judaism, Buddhism, Hinduism, Zoroastrianism, Suduanism (Jainism), Shinto, Taoism, Confucianism, and “our religion.” The monotheism he found in them all had been derived, directly or indirectly, from the missionaries of Machiventa Melchizedek, who had gone out from Salem to carry the doctrine of one God, the Most High, to the ends of the earth. Ganid was shocked to discover how near Buddhism had come to being a great religion without God. The manuscript was preserved in India for hundreds of years after his death.
ch14.b024: Last he wrote down the belief he had reached through Jesus’ teaching, which he liked to call “our religion.” It began: “⟦Q 131:10.2⟧The Lord our God is one Lord, and you should love him with all your mind and heart while you do your very best to love all his children as you love yourself.⟦/Q⟧” And it closed:

ch14.b025.en: “Though I see God in these other religions, I find him in ‘our religion’ as being more beautiful, loving, merciful, personal, and positive. But most of all, this great and glorious Being is my spiritual Father; I am his child. … At last I have a religion with a God, a marvelous God, and he is a God of eternal salvation.”

ch14.b026: The Lakes of Northern Italy and the Swiss Mountains
ch14.b027: Jesus, Gonod, and Ganid made five trips from Rome into the surrounding country. On the way up to the northern Italian lakes they met a thoughtless pagan, and Ganid was surprised that Jesus did not draw him into conversation as usual. Jesus explained: “⟦Q 132:7.2⟧Ganid, the man was not hungry for truth. He was not dissatisfied with himself. He was not ready to ask for help, and the eyes of his mind were not open to receive light for the soul. … You cannot reveal God to those who do not seek for him; you cannot lead unwilling souls into the joys of salvation. … If we know God, our real business on earth is so to live as to permit the Father to reveal himself in our lives.⟦/Q⟧”
ch14.b028: Up in the mountains of Switzerland, Jesus spent a whole day talking with father and son about Buddhism. Ganid had often asked about Buddha and received evasive replies, but now Gonod asked directly, and Jesus answered directly: “⟦Q 132:7.4⟧Your Buddha was much better than your Buddhism. Buddha was a great man, even a prophet to his people, but he was an orphan prophet; by that I mean that he early lost sight of his spiritual Father, the Father in heaven.⟦/Q⟧” Buddha, he said, had guided his ship of salvation right up to the entrance of the harbor, where, because of faulty charts, it ran aground. “⟦Q 132:7.5⟧You see, Gonod, Buddha knew God in spirit but failed clearly to discover him in mind; the Jews discovered God in mind but largely failed to know him in spirit.⟦/Q⟧”
ch14.b029: Then Ganid exclaimed: “⟦Q 132:7.6⟧Teacher, let’s you and I make a new religion, one good enough for India and big enough for Rome, and maybe we can trade it to the Jews for Yahweh.⟦/Q⟧” Jesus replied: “⟦Q 132:7.6⟧Ganid, religions are not made. The religions of men grow up over long periods of time, while the revelations of God flash upon earth in the lives of the men who reveal God to their fellows.⟦/Q⟧” They did not grasp the meaning of these prophetic words. That night Ganid could not sleep, and at last he said, “⟦Q 132:7.7⟧You know, father, I sometimes think Joshua is a prophet.⟦/Q⟧” His father only sleepily replied, “My son, there are others—” What a scene for the celestial intelligences: an Indian lad proposing to the Creator of a universe that they make a new religion! And though he did not know it, they were making a new and everlasting religion right then and there, the revelation of God to man through, and in, Jesus. When man goes in partnership with God, great things may, and do, happen.
